**Ruling**

When the prosecution alleges a motive for murder but does not prove that motive, the courts have held that this failure may be taken into account to set aside or reduce a death sentence imposed on the convict.

The judgment in *Abdul Jabbar v. State* (2022 P Cr L J Note 77, Sindh – Sukkur Bench) expressly states:

> “Motive—Scope—If the prosecution asserted a motive but failed to prove the same then failure on the part of prosecution might be reacted against the sentence of death passed against the convict on the charge of murder.”

The same principle is reiterated in *Nawab alias Tharo Gadani v. State* (2024 MLD 110, Sindh – Sukkur Bench), where the court observed that a failure to prove the motive “may react against a sentence of death passed against a convict on the charge of murder.”

**Application**

- **Fact required:** The prosecution must have expressly pleaded a motive in the charge (e.g., pre‑meditation, revenge) and then been unable to produce evidence establishing that motive at trial.  
- **Effect:** The appellate court may consider the lack of proof of motive as a ground to commute the death sentence to a lesser punishment, typically life imprisonment, because the motive is a crucial element in establishing the *mens rea* required for the most severe form of murder.  

**Limitations**

- The authorities above discuss the principle but do not provide a detailed procedural test or list of additional factors the court may weigh.  
- No statutory provision on this specific point is available in the materials before me; the ruling rests solely on the case law cited.  

Accordingly, based on the judgments cited, a failure by the prosecution to prove an asserted motive can be used to challenge and potentially overturn a death sentence for murder.

| Point | Authority | Holding |

The court will allow such amendment only when the proposed addition or deletion is expressed in unequivocal terms. | [SOURCE‑4] Shazia Jaffar vs General Public – “The provisions of Order VI, Rule 17, C.P.C. empower any party to a suit to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner as may be just… the applicant… is required to indicate in clear terms… the proposed addition must be provided in unequivocal terms.” |
| Order I Rule 10 (sub‑rule 4) provides that when a defendant is added, the plaint must, unless the court directs otherwise, be amended as necessary. The court may therefore order amendment of the plaint to reflect the addition of a new defendant. | [SOURCE‑1] Muhammad Saleem Naseem vs Additional District Judge – “Sub‑rule (4) of O.I, R.10… provided that where a defendant was added, the plaint would, unless the court otherwise directed, be amended in such manner as might be necessary.” |
| The court may also strike out a party under Order I Rule 10 when the party’s presence is no longer justified (e.g., an adult son no longer entitled to maintenance). | [SOURCE‑2] Muhammad Imran vs Samina Kousar – “Court may at any stage of the proceedings… order that the name of any party improperly joined… be struck out.” |

**Summary**

- Both Order VI Rule 17 and Order I Rule 10 empower the court to **add** parties when necessary for a full and just determination of the suit, and to **strike out** parties who are improperly joined.  
- The power to add or strike out parties can be exercised **at any stage** of the proceedings, either on an application or suo motu, provided the court is satisfied that the order is just.

**Ruling on Arbitration Act, 1940 – Sections 30 & 39 (Award‑setting‑aside)**  

| Point | Authority | Holding / Explanation |
|-------|-----------|-----------------------|
| **Scope of “invalid” in clause (c) of s. 30** | [SOURCE‑1] Azad J & K Govt vs Khawaja Muhammad Usman & Co. | The words “or is otherwise invalid” in clause (c) are interpreted to cover **all categories of objection** to the award, not only those expressly listed in the section. |
| **Objection to the validity of the reference to arbitration** | [SOURCE‑1] (same case) | An objection that the parties were not properly bound to arbitrate falls within the ambit of clause (c); the court may set aside the award on that ground. |
| **Timing of objections** | [SOURCE‑1] | Objections must be **raised at the time the award is filed**. If a party fails to object when the award is presented, the objection cannot be revived later in an appeal. |
| **Effect of non‑raised objections** | [SOURCE‑1] | An objection that was **not made before the arbitrator or the court** cannot be introduced on appeal; the appellate court is limited to the grounds expressly pleaded under s. 30. |
| **Separate determination of award objections** | [SOURCE‑1] | Issues relating to the validity of the award must be **decided separately** and must not be merged into the decree‑issuing process. A composite order that incorporates the award without a distinct determination is not a proper ground for setting aside the award. |
| **Section 39 – Procedure for setting aside** | [SOURCE‑2] Muhammad vs Sardul | The court may entertain an application under s. 39 only on the specific grounds listed in s. 30 (including the “otherwise invalid” clause). The procedural requirement is that the application be made **within the period prescribed by the Act** and must set out the precise ground of objection. |
| **Nature of the court’s review** | [SOURCE‑3] Trading Corporation of Pakistan Ltd. vs Messes Aslam Saeed & Co. | The court’s review is **limited to the grounds** in s. 30; an error of law by the arbitrator does **not** by itself vitiate the award unless it falls within those statutory grounds. |
| **Requirement of a “face‑on‑the‑record” invalidity** | [SOURCE‑5] Imperial Electric Co. vs Zhongxing Telecom Pak. | The award must contain an error or infirmity **apparent on its face**; the court will not re‑appraise the evidence or re‑determine the merits. |
| **Remedy for a decree‑related defect** | [SOURCE‑6] Ejaz Ali Siddique vs Irshad Ahmed | Where the decree issued on the basis of the award is defective, the appropriate remedy is **revision** under the CPC, not a fresh application under s. 39. |

### Application to the Question  

1. **All‑encompassing “invalid” language** – The phrase “or is otherwise invalid” in s. 30(c) is construed broadly; any defect in the arbitration process, including lack of a valid arbitration agreement, falls within it.  

2. **Objections must be contemporaneous** – Parties must raise any challenge to the award (including validity of the reference to arbitration) **when the award is filed**. Failure to do so bars later reliance on that ground in an appeal.  

3. **Separate adjudication** – The court must decide the validity of the award **independently** of the decree‑issuing stage. A composite order that merely incorporates the award without a distinct determination does not constitute a proper ground for setting aside.  

4. **Procedural gate‑keeping** – Under s. 39, the court’s jurisdiction to set aside is confined to the statutory grounds in s. 30; it does not extend to general errors of law or re‑evaluation of evidence.  

5. **Face‑value test** – The award must exhibit an apparent invalidity; the court will not look beyond the award’s terms to infer a defect.  

### Limitations  

- The **text of Sections 30 and 39** of the Arbitration Act, 1940 is not available in the materials before me; the above conclusions are drawn solely from the cited case law.  
- No authority in this session addresses the **exact period** for filing an application under s. 39 or the detailed procedural steps required. Those matters would need consultation of the statutory provision itself.

- It allows the High Court to **declare actions of public authorities ultra vires** and to **nullify such actions**.

query: what is the ruling on appreciation of evidence benefit of doubt
answer:
**Ruling on the Appreciation of Evidence and the Benefit of Doubt**

The courts consistently hold that the “benefit of doubt” is a substantive right of the accused, not a discretionary grace. A single circumstance that creates reasonable doubt in the mind of a prudent person is sufficient to entitle the accused to this benefit. Consequently, all favorable aspects of the prosecution’s evidence must be given to the accused, and any lingering doubt must lead to acquittal.

| Authority | Key Holding on Benefit of Doubt |
|-----------|---------------------------------|
| **[SOURCE‑1] Javed alias Shahid v. State** | The principle is “deep‑rooted”; a single reasonable doubt obliges the court to grant the benefit of doubt as a right, not as a concession. |
| **[SOURCE‑2] Asim alias Ahmad Bakhsh v. State** | Reiterates that many doubtful circumstances are not required; one reasonable doubt suffices to invoke the right to benefit of doubt. |
| **[SOURCE‑3] Farooq Ahmad v. State** | Confirms that “single circumstance which creates reasonable doubt in a prudent mind … entitles the accused to its benefit … as a matter of right.” |
| **[SOURCE‑4] Muhammad Abid Hussain v. State** | States the principle that “benefit of all doubts is to be given to the accused.” |
| **[SOURCE‑5] Muhammad Shafi v. State** | Emphasises that “the benefit of all favorable instances in the prosecution evidence must go to the accused regardless of whether he has taken any such plea or not.” |

**Interpretation**

- The benefit of doubt is **mandatory** where the evidence leaves any reasonable doubt about guilt.
- It is **not dependent** on the number or type of doubtful circumstances; a single reasonable doubt is enough.
- The rule applies **irrespective of the accused’s plea**; the court must automatically consider any favorable evidence for the accused.

**Application**

When a trial court evaluates the prosecution’s case, it must:

1. Identify whether any circumstance creates reasonable doubt in the mind of a prudent person.  
2. If such doubt exists, grant the benefit of doubt to the accused, leading to acquittal.  

These principles are derived solely from the judgments listed above; statutory provisions on the matter are not available in the materials before me.

| **Scope of “law”** – The term “law” is understood to include substantive and procedural legal rules that are duly enacted and applied. | The above judgments repeatedly state that any governmental action contrary to the procedural safeguards of the Constitution or statutory law is **illegal and void ab‑initio** (see *Bashir Ahmed* [ SOURCE‑6 ]). |
| **Application to State Action** – State authorities may not deprive a person of life, liberty, reputation or property without due process. | *Bashir Ahmed* [ SOURCE‑6 ] expressly holds that “any action by the Authority, contrary to the guarantee provided in Art 4… is illegal and void ab‑initio.” |
| **Geographical Reach** – The right extends to citizens wherever they are and to any other person who is **“for the time being in Pakistan.”** | *Muhammad Abdāl* [ SOURCE‑2 ] and *Ramzan Sugar Mills* [ SOURCE‑1 ] both emphasize that the protection applies to “every citizen, wherever he may be, and every other person for the time being in Pakistan.” |

**Summary**

The authorities uniformly rule that Article 4 of the Constitution creates an absolute, inalienable right for every individual within Pakistan’s territory (and for citizens abroad) to be dealt with only in accordance with law. Any governmental act that infringes on life, liberty, body, reputation or property without compliance with the law is void. The courts have applied this principle across a range of contexts, from tax assessments to customs enforcement and criminal proceedings.
